title: Find Minimum in Rotated Sorted Array
description: Binary search anchored to the right boundary. If `nums[mid] > nums[right]`, the rotation point — and the minimum — lies strictly right of mid. Otherwise it is at mid or left. O(log n).

conversation.intro: How an interview about this problem would actually play out. Each section has two parts: what you'd actually say out loud, and why that move matters. Tap a section to expand.

sections.title: 1. Restate & clarify
sections.prompt: Before touching code — pin down the inputs.
sections.say:
"Let me make sure I have this right: I'm given an array that was sorted ascending, then rotated some number of times, and I need to return the minimum value in O(log n). Clarifying:"

• Unique values guaranteed? (Duplicates change the algorithm to O(n) worst case — different problem.)
• Can the rotation be by 0? (i.e. the array is in original sorted order.)
• Empty array — what's the contract? Throw? Return undefined?
• Return the value, not the index, right?
sections.why: The unique-values question is the load-bearing one again — with duplicates (the Find Min II variant) the comparison `nums[m] > nums[r]` becomes ambiguous when `nums[m] == nums[r]`, and you fall back to `r--`, which is O(n) worst case. The rotation-by-zero question matters too because it's the boundary case that tests whether your loop handles the 'no rotation' degenerate: the minimum is just `nums[0]` and the algorithm must converge to index 0.

sections.title: 2. Brute force first (out loud)
sections.prompt: Name the obvious O(n) solution before you discard it.
sections.say:
"Brute force is a linear scan: `Math.min(...nums)`, or a `for` loop tracking the running min. O(n) time, O(1) space. Doesn't use the sortedness-after-rotation at all, which is the giveaway that we can do better — same as plain BS, the sorted structure is information we're throwing away."

"A cleverer brute force is 'find the rotation pivot' (where `nums[i] > nums[i+1]`) and return `nums[pivot+1]`. That's still O(n) if you scan, but it points at the optimization: if I can find the pivot in O(log n) — and I can, because of the rotated-sortedness invariant — then I get an O(log n) algorithm. And the minimum IS the pivot, so it's the same loop."
sections.why: The 'find the pivot' brute force is the bridge — it reframes the problem from 'find the min' to 'find the pivot,' which is what makes the BS structure visible. The minimum and the pivot are the same element, so a converging search for one is a search for the other. Saying this aloud signals you derived the algorithm, you didn't memorize it.

sections.title: 3. Spot the pattern
sections.prompt: What makes binary search work here without a target?
sections.say:
"Even after rotation, the array has a 'sorted-half' invariant — given indices `l`, `m`, `r`, at least one of `[l..m]` or `[m..r]` is fully sorted, and the OTHER half contains the rotation pivot (which is the minimum). I just need to figure out which half is unsorted and recurse there."

"The cleanest test: compare `nums[m]` to `nums[r]`."

"• If `nums[m] > nums[r]`, the right half `[m..r]` is NOT sorted (because the last element is smaller than the middle), so the pivot — the min — is strictly RIGHT of `m`. Set `l = m + 1`."

"• If `nums[m] <= nums[r]`, the right half IS sorted, so the pivot is at `m` or to its LEFT. Set `r = m` (NOT `m - 1`, because `m` itself could be the min)."

"Why anchor to `nums[r]` and not `nums[l]`? Because `nums[l] <= nums[m]` is true whether the array is rotated (left half sorted) OR not rotated at all (whole thing sorted) — ambiguous. `nums[m] vs nums[r]` cleanly separates the two cases."

"Loop condition is `l < r` (not `<=`) and the answer is `nums[l]` when they converge — same template as 'find the leftmost true in a monotone predicate.'"
sections.why: The 'why anchor right' question is the THE question on this problem — interviewers will probe it specifically. Saying it out loud unprompted ('left-anchor is ambiguous in the unrotated case') proves you understand WHY the canonical is structured this way, not just THAT it works. The `r = m` (not `m - 1`) discipline is the second classic bug — excluding the candidate min loses the answer. Both deserve to be flagged before you write the loop.

sections.title: 4. Trace through examples
sections.prompt: Walk a few inputs to confirm the model before writing the loop.
sections.intro: "Let me trace these to make sure both branches are right." Three cases — a rotated array with the min in the middle, an unrotated array (rotation-by-zero degenerate), and a 2-element rotation (smallest non-trivial case).

examples.note: Standard rotation — min is in the right half.
examples.trace:
l=0 r=6  m=3 nums[m]=7  nums[r]=2  7 > 2 → min is right of m: l = m+1 = 4
l=4 r=6  m=5 nums[m]=1  nums[r]=2  1 <= 2 → min at m or left: r = m = 5
l=4 r=5  m=4 nums[m]=0  nums[r]=1  0 <= 1 → min at m or left: r = m = 4
l=4 r=4  → converged → return nums[4] = 0 ✓

examples.note: No rotation — the algorithm must NOT misfire and pick something other than nums[0].
examples.trace:
l=0 r=3  m=1 nums[m]=13 nums[r]=17 13 <= 17 → r = m = 1
l=0 r=1  m=0 nums[m]=11 nums[r]=13 11 <= 13 → r = m = 0
l=0 r=0  → converged → return nums[0] = 11 ✓

examples.note: Smallest rotation — `m = floor(0+1)/2) = 0`, exercises both the half-check and the convergence.
examples.trace:
l=0 r=1  m=0 nums[m]=2  nums[r]=1  2 > 1 → min is right of m: l = m+1 = 1
l=1 r=1  → converged → return nums[1] = 1 ✓

sections.why: The unrotated trace is the one to narrate slowly — it's the case that proves the right-anchor choice was correct. The whole array is sorted, so `nums[m] <= nums[r]` is always true, the algorithm walks `r` leftward until it converges on index 0, and returns `nums[0]`. A left-anchor algorithm would also see `nums[l] <= nums[m]` always true and would have no signal to terminate correctly. The 2-element trace is the one that defends `l = m + 1` — without the `+1`, `m` stays at 0 forever and the loop never terminates.

sections.title: 5. Edge cases to mention
sections.prompt: What inputs would trip up a careless implementation?
sections.say:
"Edges worth flagging:"

• Empty array → undefined behavior by problem constraints, but `r = -1` and `l = 0` would cause `nums[l]` to be `undefined`. Defensive guard if the contract requires it.
• Single element → `l = r = 0`, loop never enters, return `nums[0]`. ✓
• No rotation (`[1,2,3,4,5]`) → already covered in the trace — algorithm converges to index 0.
• Full rotation (rotated by length, same as no rotation) → same.
• Rotation by 1 (`[2,1]` or `[5,1,2,3,4]`) → min is at index `n-1` or `1`. Covered.
• Duplicates (different problem — Find Min II) → `nums[m] == nums[r]` becomes ambiguous (the min could be in either half), and the fallback is `r--`, which degrades to O(n) worst case. Worth flagging that you'd ask before assuming uniqueness.
• Integer overflow on `(l + r) / 2` → safe in JS, but I'd write `l + ((r - l) >> 1)` in a typed language.
sections.why: The no-rotation edge is the one to mention explicitly — it's the test case that demonstrates the right-anchor algorithm degrades correctly. The duplicates flag is the senior-tier touch: the canonical assumes unique values, and articulating WHY duplicates break the bound (because `nums[m] == nums[r]` no longer tells you which half is sorted) shows you understand the algorithm's preconditions, not just its mechanics.

sections.title: 6. Complexity & wrap-up
sections.prompt: How would you defend the complexity claim?
sections.say:
"Time is O(log n) — each iteration halves the search range. The half-check is O(1), the pointer update is O(1), so each step is constant work and the loop runs at most `⌈log₂(n)⌉` times.

Space is O(1) — same three pointers as plain BS, no recursion, no auxiliary structure.

The defense is straightforward: it's plain BS with a different convergence target. Plain BS converges on a target value via equality; this converges on a pivot index by repeatedly discarding the sorted half. Same halving, same O(log n).

If you wanted to extend: Search Rotated Sorted Array uses the same 'one half is always sorted' invariant — same skeleton, but you anchor on `nums[l]` and check whether `target` lies in the sorted half, rather than converging to the pivot. Find Min in Rotated II handles duplicates with an `r--` fallback when `nums[m] == nums[r]`, accepting O(n) worst case. The three problems are siblings — same invariant, three different convergence strategies."
sections.why: Framing this as 'plain BS with a different convergence target' is the conceptual move that makes the algorithm memorable — instead of memorizing 'compare m to r, anchor right, r = m,' you remember 'I'm converging to the pivot via the always-sorted-half invariant.' Naming Search Rotated and Find Min II unprompted is the bonus that proves you see the rotated-BS family as a coherent set — three problems, one invariant, three convergence patterns. That's the template-level understanding interviewers grade for.

walkthrough.intro: Step through find-min on a rotated sorted array. Each iteration compares nums[m] to the RIGHT boundary nums[r] to decide which half holds the minimum. The state panel shows l, r, m, and the values at m and r.
trace: yield { line: 1, label: `enter function — nums=${JSON.stringify(nums)}`, state: { nums } };
yield { line: 2, label: `init l=0, r=${r}`, state: { nums, l, r } };
yield { line: 4, label: `loop check: l=${l} < r=${r} → enter`, state: { nums, l, r } };
yield { line: 5, label: `m = floor((${l}+${r})/2) = ${m}, nums[m]=${nums[m]}, nums[r]=${nums[r]}`, state: { nums, l, r, m, midVal: nums[m], rightVal: nums[r] } };
yield { line: 8, label: `nums[m]=${nums[m]} > nums[r]=${nums[r]} → min is strictly right of m: l = m+1 = ${l}`, state: { nums, l, r, m, midVal: nums[m], rightVal: nums[r] } };
yield { line: 11, label: `nums[m]=${nums[m]} <= nums[r]=${nums[r]} → min is at m or left of it: r = m = ${r} (do NOT exclude m)`, state: { nums, l, r, m, midVal: nums[m], rightVal: nums[r] } };
yield { line: 14, label: `pointers converged: l=r=${l} → return nums[l] = ${nums[l]}`, state: { nums, l, r, returns: nums[l] } };

notes: Compare against `nums[r]`, not `nums[l]` — comparing to left is ambiguous when the array isn't rotated.
Loop condition is `l < r` (not `<=`) and the answer is `nums[l]` when they converge.
When `nums[m] <= nums[r]`, the right half (including m) is sorted — set `r = m`, NOT `m - 1`, because m itself could be the min.
reference.crux: Compare `nums[m]` to `nums[r]` (not nums[l]): if `nums[m] > nums[r]` the min is strictly right (l=m+1), else it's at m or left (r=m) — converge on the pivot.
cruxDistractors: Linearly scan tracking the running minimum, or just return `Math.min(...nums)`.
Compare `nums[m]` to `nums[l]` to find which half is sorted, then recurse into the unsorted half.
Binary-search for the spot where `nums[i] > nums[i+1]` and return `nums[i+1]` as the rotation point.

alternates.label: Linear scan
alternates.when: Name this before discarding it. A single pass tracking the running minimum is O(n) / O(1) and trivially correct. Use only as the brute force that motivates the O(log n) BS approach — the sortedness-after-rotation is information the linear scan ignores entirely.
notes: Correct for all inputs including duplicates — the only approach that doesn't break on Find-Min II inputs.
Ignores the rotated-sortedness invariant entirely; that wasted structure is the justification for upgrading to O(log n).
In an interview, state this first: 'O(n) linear scan works but doesn't use the sorted structure — I can do O(log n) by anchoring to nums[r].'

questions.q: Why compare nums[mid] with nums[right] instead of nums[left]?
options: `nums[l] <= nums[m]` requires `l < m`, which fails in the 2-element case where `m === l`
Comparing against right disambiguates rotated vs. non-rotated halves; comparing against left does not
Anchoring left forces an extra `nums[r]` read at the end to verify, doubling memory accesses per iteration
Right-anchor lets the loop terminate with `r = m` whereas left-anchor would require `l = m`, creating the classic infinite-loop trap
questions.explain: `nums[l] <= nums[m]` is true both when the array is rotated past `m` and when it isn't rotated at all, so it carries no signal about where the pivot is. `nums[m] > nums[r]` is true only when the descent lies to the right of `m`.

questions.q: If `nums[mid] > nums[right]`, where is the minimum?
options: At mid itself, since mid is the largest element seen so far on the left side
Strictly to the right of mid: (mid..r]
At index r — `nums[r]` is smaller than `nums[mid]`, so it must already be the min
questions.explain: `nums[m]` exceeding the last element means the descent happens somewhere after `m`, so `m` itself cannot be the minimum — that is why this branch is `l = m + 1` and not `l = m`. `nums[r]` need not be the min either; on `[4,5,6,7,0,1,2]` at m=3 it's 2, but 0 is smaller.

questions.q: When `nums[mid] <= nums[right]`, why do we set `r = m` and not `r = m - 1`?
options: `r = m - 1` would skip past the pivot when the right half is exactly 2 elements long
mid itself could be the minimum — excluding it would lose the answer
`r = m - 1` paired with `l < r` makes the loop terminate one iteration early on odd-length ranges
Setting `r = m - 1` would discard the only sorted half, leaving the unsorted half to search — the opposite of the intent
questions.explain: `[m..r]` being ascending makes `nums[m]` the smallest of that half, and it may be the global minimum — excluding it loses the answer. On `[4,5,1,2,3]` the `r = m - 1` variant returns 4 instead of 1.
Every iteration discards either `[l..m]` or `(m..r]` after O(1) work, so the window halves each step. Having no target to match against changes only the stopping rule (`l < r`), not the halving.

exercises.prompt: Fill in find-min for a rotated sorted array.

blanks.hint: do not exclude mid — it could be the min

L3.prompt: Write `findMin(nums)` returning the minimum of a rotated sorted array with unique values. Log it for `[4,5,6,7,0,1,2]` then `[11,13,15,17]` (no rotation).
hints: Compare nums[mid] to nums[right], not nums[left].
Loop while l < r; return nums[l] when they converge.
On the `<=` branch use `r = m`, not `m - 1`.
